f: This is the largest country in Africa by land area, and the Sahara covers roughly four-fifths of it.
Its vast southern desert holds the prehistoric rock art of Tassili n'Ajjer, painted thousands of years ago.
Natural gas piped under the Mediterranean from this nation heats homes across southern Europe.
Its whitewashed capital, built up a steep hillside, is nicknamed 'the White City'.
A brutal war of independence from France, ending in 1962, defines this country's modern identity.
The Roman town of Timgad, laid out on a perfect grid, sits at the edge of the Sahara here.
Albert Camus was born in this country and set 'The Stranger' in its capital.
'The Battle of Algiers', filmed in this country's old Ottoman quarter, remains a classic of guerrilla cinema.
Saint Augustine was born in this territory and served as bishop of its coastal city of Hippo.
It nationalised its oil and gas in 1971, creating the state company that still funds the government.
Oil accounts for around 90% of this Portuguese-speaking nation's exports.
Its seaside capital has repeatedly been ranked the world's most expensive city for expatriate workers.
The giant sable antelope, thought extinct for decades, is this country's national symbol.
A 27-year civil war ended here in 2002, one of Africa's longest.
Kizomba, a slow partner dance now popular worldwide, originated in this country.
The Kingdom of Kongo, which exchanged ambassadors with Rome in the 1500s, straddled this country's north.
Queen Njinga fought Portuguese slavers here for four decades in the 17th century.
The Benguela railway crosses it to carry copper from Zambia and Congo to the Atlantic.
Kalandula Falls, among Africa's largest by volume, thunders over a horseshoe cliff here.

BJ.capNote: Official capital; Cotonou is the seat of government and largest city.
f: This West African nation is widely considered the birthplace of the Vodun religion, which crossed the Atlantic as voodoo.
The Kingdom of Dahomey here fielded an all-female regiment of warriors known as the Agojie.
Ganvié, a village of thousands of stilt houses, sits on a lagoon in this country.
Cotton is the dominant export of this narrow country wedged between Togo and Nigeria.
The royal palaces of Abomey, seat of a slave-trading kingdom, are a World Heritage site here.
France returned 26 looted royal treasures to this country in 2021.
A 'Door of No Return' on its beach at Ouidah marks where captives were shipped to the Americas.
Its Pendjari park is one of West Africa's last strongholds for lions and elephants.
Angelique Kidjo, winner of five Grammy awards, was born here.
A Marxist-Leninist regime ruled this country from 1975 until it abandoned communism in 1990.
Diamonds transformed this nation from one of the world's poorest at independence into a middle-income country.
The Okavango River empties into an inland delta here instead of reaching the sea.
Its currency, the pula, is named after the word for 'rain', a precious thing in the Kalahari.
It holds the largest elephant population of any country on Earth.
Alexander McCall Smith set his 'No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency' novels in this country.
The San people here carry some of the deepest genetic roots of any living human population.
It has held multiparty elections without a break since 1966, one of Africa's longest unbroken records.
The Makgadikgadi pans here are among the world's largest salt flats, the bed of a vanished lake.
A 1,109-carat stone, the second-largest gem diamond ever found, came out of a mine here in 2015.
Its first president caused an imperial scandal in the 1940s by marrying a white Englishwoman.
This country's name, adopted in 1984, translates roughly as 'land of upright people'.
FESPACO, the largest African film festival, is held in its capital every two years.
Its capital city's name, Ouagadougou, is one of the most distinctive in Africa.
Cotton is king in this landlocked Sahel nation, whose revolutionary leader Thomas Sankara was killed in 1987.
The stone ruins of Loropeni, linked to the trans-Saharan gold trade, are its only cultural World Heritage site.
The Mossi kingdoms held out here for centuries before French troops arrived in the 1890s.
It was called Upper Volta until 1984, after the three rivers that cross it.
Gold overtook cotton in the 2010s to become this country's leading export.
Two coups in the single year of 2022 brought young army officers to power here.
Its second city, Bobo-Dioulasso, has a mud-brick grand mosque bristling with wooden stakes.
The royal drummers of this tiny, densely populated country perform a ritual recognized by UNESCO.
Coffee and tea make up the bulk of exports from this landlocked nation on Lake Tanganyika.
It shares a deeply intertwined history and ethnic makeup with Rwanda, its northern neighbour.
One claimed southernmost source of the Nile lies in this small country's hills.
It was governed with Rwanda as one Belgian territory until both became independent in 1962.
Its capital moved inland to Gitega in 2019, leaving the lakeside city as the commercial hub.
The lake on its western edge is the world's second-deepest, after Baikal.
It regularly ranks among the poorest countries on Earth by income per person.
A civil war here between 1993 and 2005 killed an estimated 300,000 people.
Its monarchy, headed by a ruler titled the mwami, was abolished in 1966.
Geographers call this country 'Africa in miniature' because it contains desert, rainforest, savanna, mountains and coast.
Its national football team is nicknamed the Indomitable Lions, and Roger Milla danced at the corner flag for them.
An active volcano shares its name with this country and is West Africa's highest peak.
It is one of the few African nations with both French and English as official languages.
In 1986 a crater lake here belched a cloud of carbon dioxide that suffocated more than 1,700 people.
Its two English-speaking regions, once ruled from London, are at the heart of an armed separatist conflict.
Germany colonised this territory in 1884 and lost it to Britain and France in the First World War.
In 1990 its footballers became the first African side to reach a World Cup quarterfinal.
The Korup rainforest here is among the oldest and most species-rich in Africa.
Manu Dibango's 'Soul Makossa', an ancestor of disco, came out of this country in 1972.
This volcanic archipelago sits in the Atlantic several hundred kilometres west of Senegal.

More people of this nation's descent live abroad than in the country itself.
Its active volcano, Pico do Fogo, rises from a dramatic crater on one of its islands.
Uninhabited when the Portuguese landed in 1456, this archipelago became an Atlantic slave-trading depot.

Charles Darwin made his first landfall of the Beagle voyage on these islands in 1832.

Jean-Bédel Bokassa crowned himself emperor of this country in a lavish 1977 ceremony.

Cloves and vanilla grow alongside the perfume crops on its islands.

Livingstone's fruit bat, with a wingspan near 1.4 metres, survives only on two of its islands.

Its capital sits not on the mainland but on a volcanic island offshore.
Offshore oil made it, on paper, one of Africa's richest countries per person.

Portugal handed these territories to Spain in 1778 in exchange for land in South America.

Its capital is a UNESCO site for one of the world's best-preserved collections of Italian Art Deco architecture.
Indefinite national service has driven huge numbers of its young people to flee.

The Dahlak Archipelago, more than a hundred islands, lies off this country's coast.
A border war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 killed tens of thousands over a barren frontier town.
A peace deal with its southern neighbour in 2018 won that neighbour's prime minister a Nobel Prize.
Italy took this coast as its first colony in 1890 and used it to launch invasions inland.
Its capital sits on a plateau some 2,300 metres up, reached by a switchback climb from the sea.

SZ.capNote: Administrative capital; Lobamba is the legislative and royal capital.
f: This country changed its name in 2018 to stop being confused with Switzerland.
It is one of the world's last absolute monarchies, ruled by a king with sweeping powers.
The Umhlanga Reed Dance gathers tens of thousands of young women here each year.
This tiny kingdom is almost entirely surrounded by South Africa, touching Mozambique on one side.

Loango National Park here is famous for elephants and hippos on Atlantic beaches.

Kofi Annan, Secretary-General of the United Nations from 1997 to 2006, was born here.
No country's land lies closer to the point where the equator crosses the prime meridian.

Its state dance troupe was the first national ballet company in Africa.
Cashew nuts make up the overwhelming majority of this small country's exports.
The Bijagós Archipelago off its coast is a biosphere reserve with saltwater hippos.
It is one of the few Portuguese-speaking countries in West Africa.
Chronic coups have earned it a reputation as a hub for cocaine transiting to Europe.
Amilcar Cabral led a guerrilla war here and was assassinated months before independence took hold.
It won its freedom under the same liberation movement as Cape Verde, and the two nearly united.
A Portuguese-based creole, not Portuguese itself, is the everyday language of the street here.
No elected president has ever completed a full term in this country.
Rice grown in tidal mangrove paddies is the staple food here.
Its island societies keep a matrilineal tradition in which women choose their husbands.

CI.capNote: Official capital since 1983; Abidjan remains the largest city and economic hub.
f: This nation grows more cocoa than any other country, roughly 40% of the world's supply.
The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace here is the largest church building in the world.
Its economic capital, Abidjan, is a skyscraper-filled lagoon city sometimes called the Manhattan of the tropics.
Didier Drogba is this country's most famous footballer, and its team is nicknamed the Elephants.

Chimpanzees crack nuts with stone tools in its Tai forest, one of West Africa's last primary rainforests.

Its shallow Rift Valley lakes turn pink with millions of flamingos.
Cut flowers flown to Europe overnight are among this country's biggest earners.
This mountainous kingdom is entirely surrounded by a single other country.

Its Letseng mine, the highest diamond mine in the world, yields some of the largest stones ever found.
A conical straw hat, worn as a national symbol, sits at the centre of its flag.
Snow closes its passes in winter, and southern Africa's only ski resort operates here.
This country was founded in the 1820s as a settlement for freed American slaves.
Its flag deliberately resembles the Stars and Stripes but carries a single star.
More merchant ships fly this nation's flag of convenience than almost any other.
Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became Africa's first elected woman head of state here in 2006.
Its capital is named after an American president.
Declaring independence in 1847, it is Africa's oldest republic.
A rubber plantation opened here in 1926 was for decades the largest in the world.
Two civil wars between 1989 and 2003 killed roughly a quarter of a million people here.
A former president of this country was convicted of war crimes for arming rebels next door.
The only African footballer to win the Ballon d'Or later became this country's president.
Leptis Magna here is among the most complete Roman cities anywhere.
It holds Africa's largest proven oil reserves.
A colonel ruled this country for 42 years until he was overthrown and killed in 2011.
The Great Man-Made River, a huge project tapping fossil aquifers, supplies its coastal cities.
The Greek city of Cyrene, with its great temple of Apollo, was founded on this coast in 631 BC.
A 27-year-old signals officer overthrew this country's king in a bloodless 1969 coup.
Ghadames, an oasis town of mud-brick houses linked by covered alleys, is a World Heritage site here.
Rival governments in the east and the west have divided this country since 2014.
American warplanes bombed its two main cities in 1986 in reprisal for a Berlin bombing.
More than nine-tenths of it is desert, and it has no permanent rivers at all.
About 90% of the wildlife here exists nowhere else, including all the world's wild lemurs.
It produces most of the world's vanilla.
Its Avenue of the Baobabs is one of Africa's most photographed landscapes.
This is the world's fourth-largest island, and its people trace ancestry partly to Borneo.

Cyclones off the Indian Ocean strike this island several times in most years.
The elephant bird, the heaviest bird that ever lived, survived here until a few centuries ago.
This landlocked nation calls itself the 'Warm Heart of Africa'.
Its enormous lake holds more fish species than any other lake on Earth, mostly colourful cichlids.
Tobacco has long dominated exports from this narrow country.
A teenager here built a windmill from scrap to power his village, later a book and film.
David Livingstone reached its great lake in 1859 and called it a lake of stars.
Its first president made himself president for life and held power until elections in 1994.
It was known as Nyasaland under British rule.
Its courts annulled a presidential election in 2020, and the opposition won the rerun.
Its lake covers about a fifth of the country's total area.
Chambo, a fish from that lake, served with stiff maize porridge, is the national dish.
A fabled desert city here became shorthand in English for the ends of the earth.
The Great Mosque of Djenné is the world's largest mud-brick building, replastered by the whole town each year.
Mansa Musa, possibly history's richest person, ruled the empire centred here.
Ali Farka Touré made the 'desert blues' of this Sahel nation famous worldwide.
Gold is its leading export.

It gave up its claim to part of Western Sahara in 1979 after a costly war.

Sugar cane still blankets much of this Indian Ocean nation, though tourism and finance now lead.

Mark Twain quipped that heaven was copied after this island.
Dutch, then French, then British, it drives on the left while much of it speaks a French creole at home.

An 'underwater waterfall' appears off its southwest coast where sand pours over a shelf.

Chinua Achebe's 'Things Fall Apart' is set among this country's Igbo people.

Wole Soyinka, born here, became the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Odzala National Park here protects western lowland gorillas in dense rainforest.
This smaller of two neighbouring countries sharing a name gained independence from France in 1960.

Peatlands straddling its border with its larger namesake store billions of tonnes of carbon.
Denis Sassou Nguesso has led this country for most of the time since 1979.
This nation is known as the 'Land of a Thousand Hills'.
A genocide here in 1994 killed around 800,000 people in about a hundred days.
Mountain gorilla trekking in its volcanic north is a major source of tourism income.
It banned plastic bags in 2008 and its capital is often called Africa's cleanest city.
Women hold more than 60% of the seats in its parliament, the highest share of any country.
Drones have delivered blood to remote clinics here since 2016, a world first.
It joined the Commonwealth in 2009 despite never having been a British colony.
It switched the language of its schools and government from French to English in 2008.
On the last Saturday of each month, shops close for umuganda, a morning of compulsory community work.
Belgian colonists here issued identity cards fixing ethnic labels, hardening a division that later turned murderous.
The House of Slaves on Gorée Island, off its capital, is a memorial to the Atlantic slave trade.
'Teranga', a word for boundless hospitality, is this country's guiding social value.
Youssou N'Dour brought its mbalax music to a global audience.
A famous rally-raid ended for decades in this country's capital.
Lake Retba here turns bright pink from salt-loving algae.
Its first president was a poet elected to the Academie francaise.
The African Renaissance Monument outside its capital stands taller than the Statue of Liberty.
It is the only mainland West African country never to have suffered a military coup.
Its southern region, cut off from the rest by another country, has had a separatist insurgency since 1982.
Thieboudienne, a one-pot dish of fish and broken rice, is its national dish and a UNESCO listing.
The coco de mer, the largest seed in the plant kingdom, grows only on these islands.
Giant tortoises roam free on its Aldabra atoll, one of the world's largest populations.
Anse Source d'Argent, with granite boulders on white sand, is among the most photographed beaches anywhere.
This is Africa's smallest country by population, scattered across the Indian Ocean.
It has the highest income per person in Africa, built on tourism and tuna.
These islands had no human population at all until French settlers arrived in 1770.
It placed about a third of its vast ocean territory under protection in a 2020 debt-for-nature deal.
Pirates used these islands as a base in the 18th century, and treasure hunts still go on.
A 1977 coup installed a leader who ran this country as a one-party state for 15 years.
Unusually for mid-ocean islands, its largest ones are granite, fragments of an ancient continent.
'Blood diamonds' from this country's alluvial fields funded a brutal 1990s civil war.
Its capital was founded as a home for freed slaves and named for that liberty.
A vast cotton tree stood at the heart of its capital for centuries until it fell in 2023.
The 2014 Ebola epidemic hit this West African nation especially hard.
Its capital's harbour is one of the largest natural deep-water anchorages in the world.
The Royal Navy based its anti-slavery squadron here in the 19th century.
Fourah Bay College, founded here in 1827, was West Africa's first western-style university.
A mudslide off a hill above its capital killed more than a thousand people in 2017.
Tiwai Island here holds one of the densest concentrations of primates anywhere on Earth.
British paratroopers intervened here in 2000 to halt a rebel advance on the capital.
It has the longest mainland coastline in Africa, wrapping around the Horn.
This country keeps the world's largest camel herd.
Frankincense and myrrh have been harvested from its trees since antiquity.
Piracy off its coast dominated shipping news in the late 2000s.
It has had no effective central government for long stretches since 1991.
Its northern region declared independence in 1991 and runs its own currency and elections, recognised by nobody.
A 1993 street battle in its capital, later filmed as 'Black Hawk Down', drove American forces out.
The Laas Geel caves here hold some of Africa's best-preserved rock paintings.
Almost everyone here speaks one language and follows one religion, unusual on this continent.
The militant group al-Shabaab has fought its government since 2006.

ZA.capNote: Executive capital; Cape Town is legislative and Bloemfontein judicial.
f: This is the only country in the world with three capital cities.
A flat-topped mountain overlooks its legislative capital and a notorious prison island.
Apartheid ended here in 1994 when Nelson Mandela became president.
It has produced most of the gold ever mined and leads the world in platinum.
Rooibos tea grows only in this country's Cederberg region.
Its rugby team, the Springboks, has won the World Cup a record four times.
The world's first human heart transplant was performed in this country in 1967.
It built nuclear weapons and then dismantled them, the only nation ever to give them up voluntarily.
Caves near its largest city, called the Cradle of Humankind, hold some of the richest hominin fossil beds on Earth.
It recognises eleven official languages, and added sign language as a twelfth in 2023.
This is the world's youngest country, having voted for independence in 2011.
It holds most of the oil of the nation it split from, but must pipe it north to export.
The Sudd, one of the world's largest wetlands, spreads across it.
Cattle are central to the wealth and culture of its Dinka and Nuer peoples.
It has among the fewest kilometres of paved road of any country its size.
Civil war broke out here two years after independence and killed close to 400,000 people.
The White Nile runs the length of this country on its way north.
An antelope migration here, of white-eared kob and tiang, rivals the Serengeti in sheer numbers.
It made English its official language, unlike the Arabic-speaking state it broke away from.
Its Mundari herders wash in ash and cattle urine to keep insects off themselves and their prized cows.
This country has more pyramids than Egypt, built by the Kingdom of Kush at Meroë.
It supplies most of the world's gum arabic, an ingredient in soft drinks and sweets.
The Blue and White Nile meet at its capital.
It lost a third of its territory and most of its oil when its south seceded in 2011.
It was the largest country in Africa by area until 2011.
An uprising in 2019 toppled a president wanted by the International Criminal Court after 30 years in power.
War between the army and a paramilitary force broke out in its capital in 2023 and emptied the city.
Its western region gave its name to a conflict that killed hundreds of thousands from 2003.
Its Nubian kings once conquered Egypt and ruled it as the 25th dynasty.
Britain and Egypt governed it jointly until it became independent in 1956.
This two-island nation in the Gulf of Guinea sits almost exactly on the equator.
Once the world's largest cocoa producer, its plantation houses still stand in the jungle.
It is Africa's second-smallest country by both area and population.
Portuguese is spoken on these islands, uninhabited before European arrival.
A 1919 eclipse observed from one of these islands gave Einstein's theory of relativity its first proof.
A 1953 massacre of forced labourers on its plantations is the darkest date in its calendar.
Its forests hold the world's smallest ibis and a string of other birds found nowhere else.
A volcanic needle called Pico Cao Grande rises 300 metres straight out of its jungle.
It was a one-party socialist state until it held multiparty elections in 1991.
Oil in its waters has been promised for decades and never produced.

TZ.capNote: Official capital since 1974; Dar es Salaam is the largest city.
f: Africa's highest mountain, a free-standing snow-capped volcano, rises in this country.
The Serengeti plains and Ngorongoro Crater are its most famous parks.
A spice island archipelago, once a clove and slave-trading hub, is part of this nation.
Swahili is its national language, used across much of East Africa.
Olduvai Gorge here yielded some of the earliest human fossils ever found.
It was created in 1964 by the union of a mainland republic with an island one.
Its first president moved millions of people into collective villages under a policy called ujamaa.
Freddie Mercury was born on this country's spice island in 1946.
The Hadza people here are among the last full-time hunter-gatherers on Earth.
A violet-blue gemstone found nowhere else on Earth is mined at the foot of its highest mountain.
This is mainland Africa's smallest country, a thin ribbon of land following a river.
It is almost entirely surrounded by Senegal, opening only to the Atlantic.
Alex Haley traced his 'Roots' ancestry to Kunta Kinteh Island here.
Peanuts have long been the dominant export of this sliver of a nation.
Legend says its borders were fixed by how far a British gunboat could fire from the river.
A president who seized power in 1994 refused to accept defeat in 2016 and fled when regional troops crossed the border.
It formed a short-lived confederation with its surrounding neighbour in the 1980s.
It declared itself an Islamic republic in 2015 and reversed the decision two years later.
More than 500 bird species have been recorded in this tiny country, drawing birdwatchers all winter.
Package holidays on its short Atlantic shore earned it the nickname 'the smiling coast'.
This narrow strip of a country stretches inland from a short Gulf of Guinea coast.
Phosphate mining is its main mineral export.
The Batammariba people here build fortified mud tower-houses at Koutammakou.
Its capital sits right on the border with Ghana, unusual for a national capital.
Germany ran this narrow strip as a model colony until Britain and France divided it in the First World War.
One family has held the presidency here without a break since 1967.
A market in its capital sells skulls, skins and herbs for use in voodoo ritual.
It became independent in 1960 after a plebiscite supervised by the United Nations.
Women traders known as the Nana Benz built fortunes here selling wax-print cloth.
Its football team's bus was ambushed in Angola on the way to the 2010 Africa Cup of Nations.
The ruins of Carthage, Rome's great rival, lie just outside its capital.
Star Wars filmed Luke Skywalker's desert home here, borrowing a local town's name for the planet.
The Arab Spring began in this country in December 2010.
It is a major olive oil producer, with groves covering much of its interior.
The amphitheatre at El Djem here is one of the largest surviving from the Roman world.
Hannibal set out from a city on this coast to cross the Alps with elephants.
It was the first country in the Arab world to abolish slavery, in 1846.
A 1956 family law here gave women rights unmatched anywhere else in the Arab world.
A quartet of trade unions and civic groups from this country won the 2015 Nobel Peace Prize.
One of the world's oldest synagogues stands on an island off its southern coast.
Churchill called this landlocked country the 'Pearl of Africa'.
The White Nile begins its journey at Jinja here, flowing out of Lake Victoria.
Half the world's remaining mountain gorillas live in its Bwindi Impenetrable Forest.
Idi Amin's brutal 1970s rule, and the Entebbe hostage raid, happened here.
Glaciers survive on the equator in the range along its western border, the fabled Mountains of the Moon.
Tens of thousands of Asians expelled from here in 1972 rebuilt their lives in Britain.
A kingdom whose ceremonial king still reigns gave this country its name.
Its median age is around 16, one of the youngest populations in the world.
It shelters more refugees than any other African country.
A perch introduced to its great lake in the 1950s wiped out hundreds of native fish species.
Copper from its 'Copperbelt' has dominated this landlocked country's economy for a century.
It shares a thundering waterfall, one of the world's largest, with its southern neighbour.
Devil's Pool, where swimmers sit at the very lip of that waterfall, is on this side of the border.
It takes its name from the great river along its southern edge.
It was called Northern Rhodesia before independence in 1964.
Its first president governed for 27 years and then handed over power after losing an election.
In 2020 it became the first African country to default on its debt during the pandemic.
A Chinese-built railway to the Tanzanian coast gave this landlocked country a route to the sea in the 1970s.
The walking safari, on foot rather than in a vehicle, was invented in its Luangwa valley.
The largest known bat migration on Earth fills a patch of its swamp forest each November.
Massive dry-stone ruins built by a medieval kingdom gave this country its name.
Hyperinflation here in 2008 led to banknotes denominated in the trillions.
Robert Mugabe ruled this nation for 37 years until a 2017 coup.
Tobacco is its most valuable agricultural export.
Cecil, a lion killed by a trophy hunter in 2015, lived in its Hwange park.
It was called Rhodesia after its white minority government unilaterally declared independence in 1965.
The Great Dyke running through it holds the world's second-largest platinum reserves.
A dam built here in the 1950s created the largest reservoir on Earth by volume.
A land seizure drive from 2000 took over white-owned commercial farms and collapsed food production.
Shona artists here carve serpentine stone into sculpture sold in galleries around the world.
The Bamiyan Buddhas, carved into a cliff here, were destroyed by the Taliban in 2001.
This landlocked country supplies most of the world's lapis lazuli, mined for over 6,000 years.
It has been called the 'graveyard of empires' after wars with Britain, the Soviet Union and the United States.
The Khyber Pass connects it to Pakistan through the Hindu Kush mountains.
Buzkashi, a horseback game played with a goat carcass, is its national sport.
Alexander the Great married Roxana here and left a string of cities across its north.
Balkh, a Silk Road city in this country, was known to travellers as the mother of all cities.
The Minaret of Jam, 65 metres of decorated brick, stands alone in a remote valley here.
It long grew most of the world's opium, until a ban in 2022 cut the crop sharply.
Girls here were barred from secondary school after the government changed hands in 2021.
In 301 AD this became the first nation to adopt Christianity as its state religion.
Mount Ararat is its national symbol, though the peak lies just across the Turkish border.
Its unique 39-letter alphabet was invented in 405 AD and is still used today.
Apricots are so associated with this country that the fruit's Latin name references it.
Khachkars, intricately carved stone crosses, dot its landscape by the thousand.
Up to 1.5 million of its people were killed in an Ottoman campaign beginning in 1915.
The Matenadaran in its capital holds one of the world's great collections of medieval manuscripts.
Its capital was founded as a fortress in 782 BC, making it older than Rome.
The duduk, a mournful double-reed flute carved from apricot wood, is its signature instrument.
More of its people live outside the country than within it.
It is called the 'Land of Fire' for natural gas vents that have burned on its hillsides for centuries.
Oil from its capital's peninsula supplied roughly half the world's supply around 1900.
Its capital's Flame Towers overlook the Caspian Sea.
Caviar from Caspian sturgeon is a traditional luxury export of this country.
It fought two wars with Armenia over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.
Its Turkic language has more speakers across the border in Iran than at home.
Gobustan here holds 6,000 rock carvings of boats, hunters and dancers.
From 1918 to 1920 it was the first secular democratic republic in the Muslim world.
It has more mud volcanoes than any other country, hundreds of them bubbling across its plains.
A pipeline opened in 2006 carries its oil to the Mediterranean through Georgia and Turkey.
This island nation is connected to Saudi Arabia by a 25-kilometre causeway.
It was the first Gulf state to strike oil, in 1932, and the first to look beyond it.
It hosts the Gulf's first Formula One Grand Prix, run partly under floodlights.
Natural pearls from its waters were the region's main wealth before oil.
It is the smallest country in the Arab world by area.
The Dilmun civilisation flourished here 4,000 years ago and left tens of thousands of burial mounds.
Its name means 'two seas' in Arabic.
The United States Navy's Fifth Fleet is headquartered in this country.
Protests here in 2011 were put down with the help of Saudi troops driven across the causeway.
A single tree survives alone in its desert, fed by no water source anyone can find.
This is the world's most densely populated large country, built on a vast river delta.
It is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China.
The Sundarbans mangrove forest here shelters the largest population of Bengal tigers.
Muhammad Yunus won a Nobel Prize for pioneering microcredit in this nation.
It won independence from Pakistan in a bloody 1971 war.
Students shot here in 1952 for demanding their language are commemorated by International Mother Language Day.
A factory building collapsed here in 2013, killing more than 1,100 garment workers.
Cox's Bazar here is often described as the world's longest natural sea beach.
It shelters around a million Rohingya refugees who fled across its southeastern border.
One poet wrote the words of both this country's national anthem and India's.
This Himalayan kingdom measures Gross National Happiness alongside economic output.
It is carbon negative, absorbing more greenhouse gas than it emits.
The Tiger's Nest monastery clings to a cliff face 900 metres above the valley floor here.
Television and the internet were only permitted in this country in 1999.
Its flag features a white dragon, and its name means 'Land of the Thunder Dragon'.
Its king gave up absolute power voluntarily and introduced parliamentary democracy in 2008.
Visitors here must pay a daily sustainability fee on top of all other costs.
Archery is its national sport, shot at targets more than 140 metres away.
It has no diplomatic relations with any permanent member of the UN Security Council.
Its national dish is chillies cooked in cheese, treated as a vegetable rather than a seasoning.
This tiny, oil-rich sultanate is split into two parts by the Malaysian state of Sarawak.
Its sultan is one of the world's wealthiest monarchs and among its longest-reigning.
Kampong Ayer, a centuries-old water village on stilts, sits in its capital.
It is the only sovereign state entirely on the island of Borneo.
Its official name ends in words meaning 'abode of peace'.
It stayed a British protectorate until 1984, among the last in Asia.
Its sultanate once claimed much of Borneo and parts of the Philippines.
It adopted a strict sharia criminal code in 2014, prompting international boycotts.
A golden-domed mosque sits in a lagoon in its capital with a replica royal barge moored beside it.
It levies no income tax and provides free healthcare and education.
The world's largest religious monument, a 12th-century temple complex, is on this country's flag.
The Khmer Rouge emptied its cities in 1975, killing roughly a quarter of the population.
Its Tonlé Sap river reverses direction twice a year with the monsoon.
Garments and footwear dominate exports from this Southeast Asian nation.
Trees grow through the ruins of Ta Prohm here, familiar from Tomb Raider.
Its great temple complex was built for Hindu gods before it became a Buddhist site.
The capital of the empire that built those temples may have been the largest pre-industrial city on Earth.
The US dollar circulates alongside its own currency and is used for most large purchases.
Giant African rats are trained here to sniff out landmines left by decades of war.
Pepper grown around Kampot in its south carries a protected geographic designation.
A fortification here, built over centuries, stretches more than 20,000 kilometres.
This country invented paper, printing, gunpowder and the compass.
It manufactures more goods than any other nation and is the world's largest exporter.
An army of some 8,000 terracotta soldiers guards an emperor's tomb here.
Giant pandas live in the wild only in this country's bamboo forests.
Its high-speed rail network is longer than all others in the world combined.
The Grand Canal here, begun 2,500 years ago, is the longest artificial waterway ever dug.
It spans five geographic time zones but keeps a single official clock.
A one-child policy applied here from 1980 to 2015 and has since been replaced by pleas to have three.
Admiral Zheng He sailed treasure fleets from here as far as Africa decades before Columbus set out.
This island has been divided since 1974, and its capital is the last in Europe split by a buffer zone.
Greek myth says Aphrodite rose from the sea foam off this island's coast.
Halloumi, a squeaky cheese that grills without melting, comes from here.
Copper was mined here in antiquity, and the metal's name derives from the island's.
It joined the European Union in 2004, though EU law is suspended in the third it does not control.
British sovereign base areas still cover about 3% of this island.
Only Turkey recognises the breakaway state in its north.
Commandaria, made here, may be the oldest named wine still in production anywhere.
A whole beach resort here has stood fenced off and empty since 1974.
A cat buried beside a human here 9,500 years ago is the oldest evidence of cats living with people.
Archaeologists trace winemaking back 8,000 years here, in buried clay vessels called qvevri.
Its distinctive alphabet, one of only 14 in the world, looks like nothing else.
Khachapuri, a boat of bread filled with cheese and a raw egg yolk, is its national dish.
Stalin was born in this Caucasus country.
Its cave city of Uplistsikhe and hilltop monasteries draw visitors to the Caucasus.
Russia recognised two breakaway regions here after a short war in 2008.
Its feasts are run by a designated toastmaster called a tamada, who sets the order of toasts.
The deepest known cave on Earth drops more than two kilometres into this country's mountains.
Medieval stone defensive towers stand beside houses throughout its Svaneti highlands.
A queen ruled this country at its medieval peak and is venerated as a saint.
A white marble mausoleum built by an emperor for his wife stands in this country.
It is the world's most populous nation and its largest democracy.
It grows more spices, milk and bananas than any other country.
Chess, the decimal zero and the game that became snakes and ladders all originated here.
Its film industry, centred in Mumbai, sells more cinema tickets than any other.
Cricket is a national obsession here, with the sport's richest league.
It has 22 scheduled languages, and its banknotes print the value in 17 of them.
In 2023 it became the first country to land a craft near the Moon's south pole.
Its railway carries over 20 million passengers a day and is among the largest employers on Earth.
Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism all began in this country.
This country is spread across roughly 17,000 islands, more than any other nation.
Krakatoa erupted here in 1883 with a bang heard 4,800 kilometres away.
It is the world's most populous Muslim-majority country.
Komodo dragons, the largest living lizards, exist in the wild only here.
It produces more palm oil than the rest of the world combined.
It is building a brand-new capital city on Borneo because the current one is sinking.
A volcano here erupted in 1815 and gave the northern hemisphere a year without a summer.
Borobudur, the largest Buddhist temple in the world, rises from a plain here.
More than 700 living languages are spoken here, second only to Papua New Guinea.
The Wallace Line runs through this archipelago, splitting Asian wildlife from Australasian.
Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of an ancient empire, lies in ruins here.
This country produces most of the world's saffron, the costliest spice by weight.
Hand-knotted Persian carpets are its most famous traditional export.
A 1979 revolution replaced its monarchy with an Islamic republic.
Its blue-tiled mosques at Isfahan surround one of the world's largest public squares.
Pistachios from here are prized worldwide.
A clay cylinder from here, made for Cyrus the Great, is sometimes called an early charter of rights.
It holds the world's second-largest proven reserves of natural gas.
Nowruz, the spring new year kept here for three thousand years, is now celebrated across Central Asia.
Underground channels called qanats have carried water across its deserts for thousands of years.
Writing was invented in this land between two rivers, in ancient Mesopotamia.
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were said to stand here.
Hammurabi's law code, one of the earliest written legal systems, came from this territory.
It holds some of the world's largest proven oil reserves.
A 2003 invasion toppled Saddam Hussein in this country.
The wheel, the plough and the 60-minute hour all came from civilisations in this land.
The Epic of Gilgamesh, the oldest great work of literature, was written on tablets here.
Marshes drained here to punish the people living in them are slowly being reflooded.
A House of Wisdom in its capital made this the intellectual centre of the medieval world.
The largest cemetery on Earth, holding millions of graves, spreads across a city here.

IL.capNote: Declared capital; its status is internationally disputed and most embassies are elsewhere.
f: Its lowest point, at 430 metres below sea level, is the lowest land on Earth's surface.
This country is nicknamed the 'Start-up Nation' for its density of tech companies.
Sites holy to Judaism, Christianity and Islam sit within a single walled old city here.
Drip irrigation, developed here, transformed farming in dry regions worldwide.
The kibbutz, a collective farming community, was pioneered in this nation.
The Dead Sea Scrolls were found in cliffside caves within this country in 1947.
It declared independence in 1948 and was invaded by its neighbours the following day.
Hebrew was revived here as an everyday spoken language after centuries of liturgical use only.
The cherry tomato as sold in supermarkets today was developed by researchers in this country.
Military service is compulsory here for women as well as men.
Cherry blossom season is tracked here by a nationwide forecast front moving north.
Bullet trains have run here since 1964 with average delays measured in seconds.
This country gave the world sushi, anime, karaoke and the Walkman.
It has more people over 100 years old per capita than almost anywhere.
A snow-capped, near-perfectly symmetrical volcano is its most recognisable image.
Its capital's metropolitan area is the largest in the world by population.
It sealed itself off from almost all foreigners for over two centuries until American warships arrived in 1853.
It has more than a hundred active volcanoes and records thousands of earthquakes a year.
It has roughly one vending machine for every thirty people.
Its imperial line is described as the oldest continuous hereditary monarchy in the world.
A city carved into rose-red sandstone cliffs, rediscovered in 1812, is its greatest treasure.
Wadi Rum's red desert here has doubled for Mars in many films.
It borders a sea so salty that swimmers float on the surface.
Mansaf, lamb cooked in fermented dried yoghurt, is its national dish.
It has absorbed enormous numbers of refugees from Palestine, Iraq and Syria.
Its royal family traces its descent from the Prophet Muhammad.
It is among the most water-scarce countries on Earth.
The ruins at Jerash here are among the best-preserved Roman provincial cities anywhere.
In 1994 it became only the second Arab state to sign a peace treaty with Israel.
It renounced its claim to the West Bank in 1988.
This is the world's largest landlocked country, the ninth largest overall.
Every crewed Russian and Soviet space launch has lifted off from a cosmodrome here.
It leads the world in uranium production.
The Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake, largely dried up on this country's border.
Its steppe is where horses were first domesticated, and fermented mare's milk is still drunk.
It moved its capital north in 1997 and has renamed the new city twice since.
The Soviet Union tested more than 450 nuclear weapons on this country's steppe.
It inherited the world's fourth-largest nuclear arsenal in 1991 and gave every warhead up.
The saiga antelope, with its bulbous drooping nose, survives here in its largest numbers.
Apples are thought to have originated in its foothills, and its largest city is named after them.
Iraq invaded and annexed this small oil state in 1990, triggering the Gulf War.
Retreating forces set roughly 700 of its oil wells ablaze in 1991.
Its capital's water towers, topped by blue-green spheres, are a national emblem.
It regularly records some of the highest temperatures ever measured on Earth.
Its elected parliament is the oldest and most assertive in the Gulf.
It has no rivers or lakes at all and desalinates nearly all its drinking water.
It set up the world's first sovereign wealth fund in 1953, before it was even independent.
The largest wooden ship ever built, a dhow, was constructed here in the 1990s.
It was a British protectorate until 1961.
Around seven in ten people living here are foreign nationals.
Mountains cover over 90% of this Central Asian country.
Its Lake Issyk-Kul is one of the world's largest alpine lakes and never freezes.
Nomadic herders still move to high summer pastures and live in yurts here.
The Manas epic recited here is one of the longest poems in the world.
Its flag shows a 40-rayed sun over the crown of a yurt.
Three revolutions since 2005 have each thrown out a sitting president here.
The walnut forests at Arslanbob here are the largest in the world.
A stone Silk Road caravanserai sits at 3,200 metres in its mountains, still standing after 600 years.
In 1998 it became the first Central Asian state to join the World Trade Organization.
Gold from a single mine high in its mountains has at times been a tenth of the entire economy.
This is Southeast Asia's only landlocked country.
It is the most heavily bombed country per capita in history, from the Vietnam War era.
The Plain of Jars here is scattered with thousands of giant prehistoric stone vessels.
Monks in saffron robes collect alms at dawn through the streets of Luang Prabang here.
It exports hydroelectricity from the Mekong to its neighbours, aiming to be the 'battery of Asia'.
Its old kingdom was called the Land of a Million Elephants.
It is one of the last one-party communist states in the world.
A railway opened in 2021 links its capital to the Chinese border in under four hours.
The widest waterfall in the world spreads across the Mekong in its south.
Sticky rice, eaten by hand from a woven basket, is the staple at every meal here.
A cedar tree, mentioned in the Bible and used for Phoenician ships, sits at the centre of its flag.
Its capital, once called the 'Paris of the Middle East', endured a 15-year civil war.
A massive ammonium nitrate explosion devastated its port in August 2020.
The Phoenicians, who spread the alphabet across the Mediterranean, sailed from this coast.
You can ski in its mountains and swim in the Mediterranean on the same day.
Its parliament seats and top offices are shared out by religious sect under a formula from 1943.
Baalbek here holds the largest Roman temple ruins in the world.
Its currency lost more than 98% of its value after the banks collapsed in 2019.
It hosts more refugees per head of population than any other country.
Byblos here is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities, and gave English the word 'bible'.
Twin towers linked by a skybridge were the world's tallest buildings here from 1998 to 2004.
This country is split between a peninsula and the northern third of Borneo.
It is the world's second-largest palm oil producer and a major semiconductor assembler.
The rafflesia, the world's largest single flower, blooms in its rainforests.
Flight MH370 vanished on a route from this country in 2014.
The strait along its west coast carries about a quarter of the world's traded goods.
Its head of state is chosen every five years from among nine hereditary state rulers, a rotation unique in the world.
The largest cave chamber on Earth by floor area lies under its part of Borneo.
It makes most of the world's rubber gloves.
One coalition governed here from independence in 1957 until it finally lost an election in 2018.
This is the world's lowest-lying country, averaging about 1.5 metres above sea level.
Its government once held a cabinet meeting underwater to dramatise climate change.
Nearly 1,200 coral islands make up this nation, most of them uninhabited.
Overwater bungalows on private-island resorts are its signature offering.
Tuna fishing was its main industry before tourism took over.
It converted from Buddhism to Islam in 1153, and ruins of the old temples still turn up.
The English word 'atoll' comes from the language of these islands.

Its capital island is one of the most densely populated places on Earth.
Cowrie shells gathered in its lagoons served as currency across Africa and Asia for centuries.
